_**Agent (auto-low)**_

**Unusual** means it breaks your baseline — rare, new, or out of pattern. It does not, by itself, mean something is wrong. A first-time behavior, a one-off glitch, or a legitimate edge case can all be unusual and still fine.

**Suspicious** means unusual *plus* a reason to think harm, deception, or system failure might be hiding underneath. You have a hypothesis: this doesn't fit an innocent explanation, it repeats, the stakes are high, or luck already covered a close call once.

A quick way to hold the two apart:

| | Unusual | Suspicious |
|---|---|---|
| **Question** | "Is this outside normal?" | "Should I act as if something is wrong?" |
| **Evidence** | Deviation from baseline | Deviation + motive, pattern, stakes, or mismatch |
| **Response** | Notice, maybe log | Investigate, slow down, redesign, or escalate |
| **Risk** | Treating novelty as guilt | Treating a warning as a lucky one-off |

Example: a browser loading faster than Chrome is **unusual**. A quote with oddly cheap terms is **unusual** that turns **suspicious** once you ask what the total cost is after fees.

The cleanest single verse is **John 7:24**:

> **"Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment."** (NASB)

That is the split in one line:

- **Appearance** = what looks odd on the surface (unusual timing, origin, style, credentials).
- **Righteous judgment** = a deeper read — does the teaching, motive, and fruit line up with God's word?

Context helps: at the Feast, people were thrown because Jesus did not fit their picture of Messiah (where He came from, how He taught). The crowd treated the **surprise** as grounds to dismiss Him. Jesus says: do not stop at "this looks wrong"; judge rightly.

That maps straight to your garden's [Discern His Will Daily](/notes/discern-his-will-daily/) lane (John 7:16–18 in the same chapter): willingness to obey God first, then you can tell real teaching from noise.

---

## Two passages that sharpen each side

**When unusual should not auto-trigger suspicion** — **1 Thessalonians 5:21–22**:

> "Test everything; hold fast to what is good. Abstain from every kind of evil."

Do not treat every surprise as evil. **Test** first. Then either hold what is good or refuse what is actually wrong. Unusual gets examined; only what fails the test becomes suspicious.

**When unusual surface hides real danger** — **Matthew 7:15–20** (already in [By Their Fruits](/notes/by-their-fruits/) and [Judge Not](/notes/judge-not/)):

> Wolves come in sheep's clothing… you will know them by their fruits.

The wolf is not suspicious because it looks weird — it looks **normal** (sheep). What makes it suspicious is the **mismatch over time**: smooth talk now, bitter fruit later. [Judge Not](/notes/judge-not/) keeps you from playing final judge on souls; [By Their Fruits](/notes/by-their-fruits/) still lets you read evidence.

---

## Quick map

| Verse | Unusual | Suspicious |
|-------|---------|------------|
| **John 7:24** | Surprising appearance | Fails righteous judgment after a real look |
| **1 Thess 5:21–22** | Worth testing, not auto-rejecting | Fails the test — abstain |
| **Matt 7:15–20** | Looks fine on the outside | Fruit does not match the claim |

If you want one verse to anchor a garden note, **John 7:24** is the tightest. **Matthew 7:15–20** is the best passage when the danger is disguise, not obvious oddness.
